chapters.name: Chapter 1: From military logistics to civilian supply chains

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Speaking the civilian supply-chain language
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Translate five military logistics terms into the civilian words employers use.
This lesson builds toward: Given logistics tasks from your service, you will translate military logistics terms into the civilian words employers use, with five terms translated and two matching civilian job titles.
A supply chain is every step that gets a product from where it is made to the person who uses it. Logistics is the planning and moving part of that chain.
Many military terms have civilian twins. A supply room or warehouse is inventory management. A convoy is transportation or freight. A motor pool is fleet maintenance. Class I to IX supply planning is demand planning. The last stretch to the user is called "last-mile delivery".
My Next Move for Veterans (mynextmove.org/vets), from the U.S. Department of Labor, lets you enter your military job and see similar civilian careers, such as logistician, warehouse supervisor or dispatcher.
Step by step:
- List five logistics tasks you did in service.
- Ask an AI assistant: "Translate these military logistics tasks into civilian supply-chain terms."
- Look up your military job on mynextmove.org/vets.
- Write the civilian job titles that fit best.
Words to know:
- Supply chain: every step from making a product to the person who uses it.
- Inventory: the items a business keeps in stock.
- Last-mile delivery: the final trip that brings an item to the customer.
- 3PL: third-party logistics: a company hired to store and ship goods for another business.
Official sources:
- My Next Move for Veterans (U.S. Department of Labor)
Try it now: Write five logistics tasks from your service. Ask an AI assistant to translate them into civilian terms, then look up your military job on mynextmove.org/vets and write two matching job titles.
You can now describe your military logistics work in the words civilian employers use.

options: Only the trucks a company owns
Every step from making a product to the person who uses it
A list of suppliers' phone numbers
check.why: The supply chain covers every step from production to the end user.

check.q: Your résumé says "Ran the motor pool". What civilian words do you use?
check.why: A military motor pool is closest to civilian fleet maintenance.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Where AI fits in logistics
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name four ways AI is used in logistics and the decisions people still make.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of AI in warehouses and trucking, you will describe four ways AI is used in logistics and the decision a person still makes for each, naming one thing a person must check for each.
Companies use AI to forecast demand (guess how much of an item people will need), plan routes that save fuel and time, spot late shipments early, and answer customer questions about deliveries.
AI only knows the data it is given. If the data is old, wrong or missing, the plan will be wrong too. A storm, a road closure or a holiday rush may not be in the data.
People still make the calls: checking the plan makes sense, handling exceptions, keeping drivers and workers safe, and talking to customers. That judgment is exactly what military logistics trained you to do.
Words to know:
- Forecast: a careful guess about what will happen, such as how much stock you will need.
- Route optimization: finding the best order and path for deliveries.
- Exception: something that does not go to plan, like a late truck.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "How do warehouses and trucking companies use AI today? Give four examples in simple words." Next to each, write one thing a person still has to check.
You can now explain where AI helps in logistics and where human judgment is still needed.

options: Counting stock at the end of the year
A careful guess about how much will be needed
check.why: Demand forecasting estimates how much will be needed, and AI often helps make it.

check.q: An AI route plan sends a truck down a road closed this morning. Who fixes it?
options: A person who knows about the closure
The AI will fix itself later
check.why: AI only knows the data it has, so people handle exceptions like closures.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Building an inventory reorder sheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a spreadsheet that shows when to reorder each item.
This lesson builds toward: Given daily use, lead time and safety stock for five items, you will build a spreadsheet that calculates when to reorder each item, with one row checked by hand on a calculator.
A reorder point is the stock level that tells you to order more before you run out. A simple formula is: daily use times lead time (days to get a delivery), plus safety stock (extra for surprises).
Example: a food bank uses 20 cans of beans a day, delivery takes 5 days, and it keeps 40 extra. Reorder point = 20 x 5 + 40 = 140. When stock drops to 140, order more.
An AI assistant can help you set up the columns and the spreadsheet formula. Always test the formula on one row by hand to make sure it is right.
Step by step:
- Open a blank Google Sheet or Excel workbook.
- Make columns: Item, On hand, Daily use, Lead time (days), Safety stock, Reorder point, Order now?
- Ask an AI assistant for the formula for Reorder point and for an "Order now?" yes/no column.
- Add five items with made-up numbers.
- Check one row by hand with a calculator.
Words to know:
- Reorder point: the stock level that tells you to order more.
- Lead time: how many days it takes for an order to arrive.
- Safety stock: extra stock kept for surprises.
- Formula: a calculation a spreadsheet does for you.
Try it now: Build the reorder sheet with five items. Ask an AI assistant for the formulas, then check one row with a calculator and fix anything that is wrong.
You can now build a spreadsheet that shows when each item needs to be reordered.

check.why: Safety stock covers surprises like late deliveries or extra demand.

check.q: Daily use 5, lead time 6 days, safety stock 10. What is the reorder point?
check.why: Daily use times lead time (5 x 6 = 30) plus safety stock (10) is 40.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Drafting a delivery schedule with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to draft a one-week delivery schedule and check it against real limits.
This lesson builds toward: Given stops, hours, vehicles and drivers, you will use an AI assistant to draft a one-week delivery schedule and check it against real limits, fixing every problem you find with a map app and the stop hours.
A delivery schedule says who goes where, when, with what. AI can draft one quickly if you give it the facts: stops, opening hours, number of vehicles and drivers, driver hours, and what each stop needs.
Then you check it like a convoy plan. Are travel times realistic on a real map? Are drivers getting breaks? Does any stop get a delivery when it is closed?
Use made-up or business-safe data only. Do not paste customer names, home addresses or anything your employer has not approved for AI tools.
Step by step:
- List stops, hours, vehicles, drivers and what each stop needs.
- Ask an AI assistant: "Make a one-week delivery schedule as a table with these limits."
- Check travel times on a map app.
- Check breaks, opening hours and vehicle space.
- Fix the schedule and save it next to your inventory sheet.
Words to know:
- Delivery schedule: a plan of who delivers what, where and when.
- Constraint: a limit the plan must follow, such as opening hours or driver hours.
Try it now: For a made-up food bank with three pantry stops and one van, ask an AI assistant for a one-week delivery schedule as a table. Check it on a map app and fix one problem you find.
You can now draft a delivery schedule with AI and check it against real-world limits.

check.q: What is a constraint in a delivery schedule?
options: A limit the plan must follow, like opening hours
check.why: Constraints are limits such as hours, vehicles and drivers that the schedule must respect.

check.q: The AI schedule says a 40-mile trip takes 15 minutes. What do you do?
options: Check the time in a map app and fix the schedule
Tell the driver to go faster
check.why: You check AI travel times against a map app and fix anything that is not realistic.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Spotting problems in operations data
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to summarize a small data table and confirm what it finds yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small table of delivery data, you will use AI to find patterns and confirm one yourself with a spreadsheet filter, and write the cause, a fix and how you will measure it.
Operations teams look at data every day: late deliveries, items running low, damaged goods. AI can summarize a table and point to patterns, like "Tuesday deliveries are late most often."
Treat AI findings like intel: useful, but confirm before you act. Sort or filter the spreadsheet yourself to see if the pattern is real.
When you find a real problem, write the cause you think it is, a fix, and how you will know the fix worked.
Step by step:
- Make a small table: date, stop, on time (yes/no), reason if late.
- Ask an AI assistant: "What patterns do you see in this table?"
- Sort or filter the sheet yourself to confirm.
- Write: problem, likely cause, fix, how you will measure it.
Words to know:
- Pattern: something that happens again and again in the data.
- Filter: a spreadsheet tool that shows only the rows you choose.
Try it now: Make a 10-row delivery table with some late deliveries. Ask an AI assistant for patterns, then filter the sheet yourself to confirm one, and write a fix.
You can now use AI to find a pattern in operations data and confirm it before acting.

check.q: What does a spreadsheet filter do?
options: Shows only the rows you choose
check.why: A filter hides rows you do not need so you can check a pattern yourself.

check.q: The AI says most late deliveries come from one driver. What do you do?
options: Filter the data yourself to confirm before acting
check.why: Treat AI findings like intel: useful, but confirm before acting.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Briefing the plan and finding work
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Brief an operations plan in civilian terms and connect it to your next job step.
This lesson builds toward: Using your sheet, schedule and risks, you will brief an operations plan in civilian terms and write two résumé lines about your logistics work, with the situation, plan, three risks and a backup for each.
Civilian managers like short briefs, just like commanders: the situation, the plan, the risks and the backup plans, and what you need from them. Use civilian words: "inventory", "delivery schedule", "on-time rate".
Turn your service into résumé lines with numbers, for example: "Managed inventory of 1,200 items worth $2 million with zero losses at audit." Use only numbers you can stand behind.
For job help, the Department of Labor's Veterans' Employment and Training Service (VETS) runs the Transition Assistance Program and points to apprenticeships. If you have the GI Bill, VA's on-the-job training and apprenticeship benefit can pay a monthly amount while you train with an approved employer. Check the official pages for who qualifies.
Step by step:
- Write the brief: situation, plan, risks, backups, what you need.
- Use civilian terms throughout.
- Write two résumé lines with real numbers.
- Check dol.gov/agencies/vets and the va.gov on-the-job training page for next steps.
Words to know:
- Brief: a short spoken or written summary of a plan for a decision maker.
- On-time rate: the share of deliveries that arrive when promised.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor, Veterans' Employment and Training Service
- VA: On-the-job training and apprenticeships
Try it now: Final task: put your reorder sheet, checked delivery schedule, three risks with backups, and two résumé lines into a one-page operations brief.
You can now plan inventory and deliveries with AI help, check the plan yourself, and brief it in civilian terms.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Reorder sheet Fewer than five items, or the reorder points are wrong. Five items with correct reorder points, one row checked by hand. The sheet flags items at or below the reorder point. Checked delivery schedule The AI schedule was used without checks, or breaks a limit. A one-week schedule that respects stop hours, vehicles and drivers, with travel times checked on a map app. The learner names the problem they found and how they fixed it. Risks and backups Fewer than three risks, or risks with no backup. Three risks, each with a backup plan. Each backup says who acts and when. Civilian résumé lines Lines use military terms or have no result. Two lines in civilian logistics words with a size or result. The lines match a civilian job title from My Next Move for Veterans. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What goes in a good operations brief?
options: A long story of your career
check.why: A brief gives the situation, the plan and the risks with backups, short and clear.

check.q: Which résumé line describes military logistics work best for a civilian employer?
options: "Managed 800 items worth $1M with zero losses at audit."
check.why: It uses civilian words, a size and a result.
